source.title: Nexus scissor: enhance open-access language model safety by connection pruning
source.authors: Pei-Hua Mai; You-Jia Yang; Ran Yan; Yan Pang

record.file_problem: No major file problem; some equations and tables are flattened in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a different unlearning method, Nexus Scissor, remains effective under jailbreak and fine-tuning attacks; it also evaluates a gradient-ascent unlearning comparator.
record.gate_note: The study reports ASR after Nexus Scissor under four attack types and compares ASR across evaluators. It does not test activation-direction ablation, quantization, or recovery using unrelated or loosely related examples. The figure-only category results in Fig. 7 state that reductions vary by category, especially for political lobbying and pornography, but do not provide extractable numeric values; the unLER comparison in Fig. 3 likewise gives no extractable numeric values. Hyperparameter trends and clustering comparisons are not separate results on the claim’s versions.
record.test_reason: The study proposes Nexus Scissor, an unlearning method that applies gradient ascent with a KL term to harmful knowledge-graph triplets. It reports GPT-4o-judged attack success rate (ASR) on four open models (LLaMA-2-7b, LLaMA-2-13b, LLaMA-3-8b, Phi-3-14b) under four attacks: a harmful-demonstration fine-tuning attack (BDFinetune), two prompt jailbreaks (AutoDAN, Template) and decoding manipulation (GenExploit). Each is compared with the same attack on the original model. This is a newer method's claim to resist recovery attacks, so its results bear on F. Caveats: the measure is judged harmfulness ASR, not targeted-knowledge accuracy. The forget set was extracted with the same four attacks used for evaluation, and the text describes no held-out prompt split. No ASR is given for the unlearned model before an attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report an average ASR reduction above 91% with average GLUE loss within 2%, and a better safety–utility trade-off than the unLER gradient-ascent baseline (about 5% higher utility). They say clustering raises ASR slightly (6.5%) but improves GLUE by 9.8%. The introduction and discussion say ASR is 'at least 43% lower' than unLER, while the results section gives 34–68%; the two figures disagree.
record.recipe_differences: Nexus Scissor extracts harmful responses, converts them to knowledge-graph triplets, clusters triplets, and fine-tunes with gradient ascent on selected triplets. It is compared with unLER, which applies gradient ascent to entire harmful responses.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR and utility vary with model, attack type, evaluator, pruning sample size, clustering settings, and other hyperparameters. The text also reports less pronounced harmfulness-score reductions for political lobbying and pornography categories.

fits_no_version.finding: After pruning, average GLUE accuracy stays within about 0.5–1.9% of the original model's, with per-task drops of up to 5.5 points (Phi-3 SST2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Triplet-level gradient-ascent unlearning preserves general NLU benchmark accuracy.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported tables. The evaluation uses ASR judged by harmfulness scores, rather than targeted-knowledge accuracy or a never-trained control. The paper reports evaluator comparisons, but does not show that the targeted knowledge was deleted rather than made inaccessible.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the numeric tables transcribed here. Fig. 3 unLER comparisons and Fig. 7 category-specific outcomes are not given as extractable numeric values in the supplied text; the category variation is noted in gate_note.

untested.parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy, chance-level comparison or WMDP-style probe; only judged harmfulness ASR and GLUE.

Nexus Scissor's own BDFinetune results are filed under F, because its forget set was built from this attack's outputs. The text gives no numbers for a standard method under fine-tuning (unLER, Fig. 3; see missing). Unrelated, loosely related or forget-subset relearning sets are not tested. The BDFinetune set size and number of steps are not stated.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deletion.

AutoDAN and Template results on Nexus Scissor are filed under F, because its forget set was built from these attacks' outputs. No prompt attack on a standard unlearning method is reported. Rephrasing, other languages and in-context information are not tested.

Not evaluated against quantization, activation ablation, held-out attacks or held-out prompts (no split between extraction and evaluation prompts is described), or knowledge probes beyond judged harmfulness. No ASR is reported for the unlearned model before an attack, so how much each attack recovers can't be measured.

missing.what: BDFinetune ASR and GLUE for the unLER gradient-ascent baseline. The text says Nexus Scissor's ASR is 34–68% lower than unLER's (unclear whether relative or in points), so plain GA leaves more harmful output after fine-tuning. This bears on B for a standard GA method, and on F by comparison.
missing.locator: Fig. 3 and 'Comparative studies with naive unlearning method'

missing.what: BDFinetune ASR for the non-clustering variant; clustering raises ASR by 6.5% on average.
Per-category harmfulness scores under BDFinetune on ForbidQ: the reduction is weaker for political lobbying and pornography.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) Resolved the duplicate row_fixes on r1, r3, r4, r5, r7, r8, r9, r11, r12, r15 and r16, plus r13, which also had two items. Every attack row (r1–r28) now has one item, linked to F only. A row carries one state, and the same numbers read as 'observed' for F (the method resists) but 'absent' for B or E (no recovery), so one state can't serve both versions. Linking to F alone is also the better reading of the text: the forget set was extracted with the same four attacks (and, as described, the same prompts) used to evaluate, so these results are the counter-method's own robustness claim. The studies file treats TAR the same way. Labelling B and E from the same rows would count one result twice.
(2) Dropped the earlier B 'challenges', B 'limits_scope' and E 'challenges' labels as a result, and listed B and E under untested with the reason. If Iris prefers B/E links, the same rows would read absent for the three LLaMA models and partial for Phi-3 under BDFinetune.
(3) Moved 'no ASR for the unlearned model before an attack' out of missing and into F's untested entry: the study doesn't report it, so it isn't a row the record left out.
(4) The Fig. 7 missing entry now names F only; the unLER entry keeps B, F.
(5) authors_conclusion: the '43%' figure is in the introduction and discussion, not the abstract.
Row states, the three F labels, the GLUE fits_no_version entry and A/C/D untested are unchanged except for wording. GenExploit rows (r2, r6, r10, r14) stay on F even though decoding manipulation is not among the attacks B–E list; this is a judgment call. Table 4 rows rescore the same BDFinetune outputs with other judges, so they show the result doesn't depend on the judge; they are not replications. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The text contains no instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy or chance-level result is reported; GLUE measures general-task accuracy only.

The BDFinetune attack uses explicit harmful-example demonstrations, but the number and relation of examples to forgotten facts are not stated. Unrelated or loosely related relearning sets are not tested.
No activation-direction ablation or direct test distinguishing blocked access from deletion is reported.
Tests AutoDAN and template jailbreak attacks; other languages and in-context information are not tested.
Tests Nexus Scissor against the four stated attacks, not against quantization, activation ablation, or the full range of recovery attacks in the claim.

relation.reason: Reports its own ASR results for its method under four attacks on four models.

tranche.reason: A different unlearning method (gradient ascent plus KL on clustered harmful knowledge-graph triplets) with its own ASR results under jailbreak and fine-tuning attacks. Version F is the question addressed.

source_check.notes: The forget set is built from the four test attacks on the same AdvBench prompts, so the test is in-distribution. The measure is GPT-4o-judged harmfulness ASR, not knowledge accuracy, and only BDFinetune has the four-judge check. BDFinetune settings (n examples, steps) are not stated. The text's GenExploit post-pruning average (3.46) does not match Table 2 (3.36 computed).

statements.correction: Nexus Scissor, LLaMA-2-7b/LLaMA-2-13b/LLaMA-3-8b: ASR 21.73-100.00 on the attacked originals -> 0.19-8.46 after unlearning, GPT-4o judge, all four attacks (Table 2). BDFinetune was also scored by LLaMA Guard 2, LLaMA Guard 3 and Beaver-Dam-7B: 44.42-94.81 -> 3.27-6.35 (Table 4). The other three attacks were scored by GPT-4o only. The forget set was built from the same four attacks on the same AdvBench prompts.
statements.problem: The text pairs 'four judges' with all four attacks. Only BDFinetune was scored by four judges; GenExploit, AutoDAN and Template were scored by GPT-4o only. The ranges are right.

statements.correction: Phi-3-14b BDFinetune residual ASR: 14.81 (GPT-4o), 16.15 (LLaMA Guard 2), 18.26 (LLaMA Guard 3), 14.23 (Beaver-Dam-7B), from originals of 87.69-95.77. Other three models: 3.27-6.43 (Tables 2, 4). Phi still falls by about 81-85%.
Models tested: LLaMA-2-7b, LLaMA-2-13b, LLaMA-3-8b and Phi-3-14b; none above 14B.
Nexus Scissor's ASR uses a GPT-4o harmfulness judge (score >2 out of 5 counts as success). LLaMA Guard 2, LLaMA Guard 3 and Beaver-Dam-7B are checks on BDFinetune only (Table 4).

Phi-3-14b BDFinetune ASR after Nexus Scissor: 14.81 (GPT-4o), 16.15 (LLaMA Guard 2), 18.26 (LLaMA Guard 3), 14.23 (Beaver-Dam-7B), about an 81-85% drop under every judge. Post-unlearning ASR on each model lies within about 4 points across the judges (Table 4). Only the baselines vary more, e.g. LLaMA-3-8b origin 44.04 (GPT-4o) vs 59.62 (LLaMA Guard 3). Drop the citation, or cite it as a judge-stable result.
statements.problem: The statement cites r13 and r26-r28 under the judge factor but says nothing about Nexus Scissor. Those rows show the post-unlearning reading holding across judges, not changing with them.

statements.correction: Not in the statement text. If added: BDFinetune residual ASR is 14.81 on Phi-3-14b vs 5.19-6.43 on the three LLaMA models (GPT-4o, Table 2), and 16.15 vs 3.27-4.62 under LLaMA Guard 2 (Table 4).
statements.problem: The statement cites r13 and r26 but its text does not mention Nexus Scissor. The point those rows imply (Phi weaker than the LLaMA models) is correct.
